title: Health History Assessment in Metabolic and Endocrine Disorders
path: Management of Clients with Problems of the Metabolic and Endocrine System

headings.title: Introduction to Endocrine and Metabolic Health History
headings.content: Gathering a health history for endocrine and metabolic disorders requires a systematic approach. The endocrine system regulates complex physiological processes through hormone secretion, meaning subtle imbalances often manifest across multiple unrelated body systems. When interviewing a patient with suspected metabolic dysfunction, the nurse must listen carefully for vague complaints like chronic fatigue, unexpected weight shifts, or mood alterations that point toward hormonal deregulation.

headings.title: Biographical Data and Demographic Risk Factors
headings.content:
Age, biological sex, and geographic background significantly influence endocrine disease patterns. 

- **Age**: Type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypothyroidism become increasingly prevalent in older adults, whereas type 1 diabetes typically manifests during childhood or adolescence.
- **Sex**: Autoimmune thyroid disorders show a markedly higher incidence in women.
- **Geography**: Endemic goiter remains a public health concern in regions with iodine-deficient soil, such as parts of the Nigerian hinterland.

headings.title: Chief Complaint and History of Present Illness
headings.content: Patients rarely walk into a clinic stating they have an endocrine problem; instead, they report specific functional changes. The History of Present Illness (HPI) must capture the onset, duration, severity, and triggering factors of these complaints. Common presenting triggers include polyuria, polydipsia, unexplained weight fluctuation, heat or cold intolerance, and sudden visual disturbances.

headings.title: Comprehensive Review of Systems
headings.content:
Systematic questioning helps uncover hidden metabolic shifts. The nurse screens every major body system to capture cascading endocrine effects:

| System | Assessment Focus | Potential Finding |
|---|---|---|
| Integumentary | Skin texture, hair distribution, pigmentation | Dry skin, alopecia, or velvety hyperpigmentation |
| Neurological | Cognition, reflexes, mood stability | Tremors, lethargy, anxiety, or sluggish reflexes |
| Cardiovascular | Blood pressure, heart rhythm | Hypertension, tachycardia, or bradycardia |
| Gastrointestinal | Bowel patterns, appetite changes | Constipation or frequent loose stools |

headings.title: Past Medical, Surgical, and Family History
headings.content: Previous illnesses often hold the key to current endocrine imbalances. Autoimmune diseases frequently cluster in individuals; a history of rheumatoid arthritis or pernicious anemia increases susceptibility to autoimmune thyroiditis. Surgical history requires careful review, particularly any prior neck operations, as accidental parathyroid damage during thyroidectomy causes lifelong hypocalcemia.

headings.title: Medication and Substance History
headings.content: Exogenous hormone use, herbal preparations, and over-the-counter drugs frequently disrupt endocrine feedback loops. Corticosteroids are notorious for inducing secondary Cushing's syndrome and masking infection signs. The nurse must also inquire about traditional remedies, as heavy metal content in some local preparations can impair renal and endocrine function.

headings.title: Psychosocial, Nutritional, and Lifestyle Assessment
headings.content: Endocrine function is deeply intertwined with daily habits and emotional stress. Chronic stress triggers continuous cortisol release from the adrenal cortex, exacerbating blood glucose instability and hypertension. The nurse evaluates dietary habits, sleep hygiene, alcohol intake, and physical activity levels to understand the complete picture of metabolic health.
